skills.name: Use significant figures, absolute error and relative error

note.text:
Significant figures count from the first non-zero digit. 0.004 507 to 2 s.f. is 0.0045; 38 260 to 2 s.f. is 38 000.
Zeros between non-zero digits count (4 507 has 4 s.f.); leading zeros never count (0.004 has 1 s.f.); zeros at the end after a decimal point count (0.0450 has 3 s.f.).
Absolute error = |measured value − true value|.
Relative error = absolute error ÷ true value.
For a measurement given to a unit, the maximum absolute error is half the unit: 3.4 cm to the nearest 0.1 cm has a maximum error of 0.05 cm.

sections.heading: Your goal and connections
sections.text:
By the end, you should be able to round to significant figures, count the significant figures in a number, and find absolute, relative and maximum errors.
Builds on: Lesson {32} (rounding and bounds).
Leads to: Lesson {34} (percentage error and greatest and least values) and measurement in Physics.

sections.heading: Significant figures
sections.text:
Significant figures (s.f.) start at the first non-zero digit, wherever the decimal point is.
• {0.004507} to {2} s.f.: the first two are {4} and {5}; next is {0}, so {0.0045}.
• {38260} to {2} s.f.: {3}, {8}; next {2} → {38000}. Keep the place value with zeros.
Counting: leading zeros never count; zeros between digits count; final zeros after a decimal point count. So {0.0450} has three s.f. and {4507} has four.

sections.heading: Errors
sections.text:
No measurement is perfect.
• Absolute error = |measured − true|: a table of {50} cm measured as {52} cm has an error of {2} cm.
• Relative error = absolute error ÷ true value = {2} ÷ {50} = {0.04}. It compares the error with the size: {2} cm on a table matters less than {2} cm on a pencil.
• A value given to the nearest {0.1} cm can be wrong by up to {0.05} cm: half the unit. That is the maximum absolute error.

worked_example.problem: A pupil measures a table as {m} cm; its true length is {t} cm. Find the absolute error and the relative error.
worked_example.answer: absolute error {abs(m - t)} cm; relative error {dec(abs(m - t) / t)}
